observations.text: This Institutional Performance run records 48 with band Drag, which reflects scored responses rather than whole-process effectiveness. The participant reports clarity of how their intended direction translates into day-to-day action as “Mixed: clear on some things, not others”, and reliability of decisions staying in place after they make them as “Mixed: depends who owns it”.

For this unit, the participant reports whether underlying causes of recurring organizational problems are fixed or the problems repeatedly managed as “Mixed: some fixed, many recur”, selected the pattern that the same problems keep coming back, and reports how often problems return after being addressed as “Sometimes: depends on the problem”. Reported recurrence does not establish that no fix was attempted or that a cause went unaddressed.

The participant describes the current situation in this unit as “Pressure: higher demand or stress” and the strain over the past year on the organization behind these results as “About the same”. Dependence of results on extra effort to make up for weaknesses in how the organization operates is reported as “Moderately: some extra effort makes up for gaps”, and management intervention needed to maintain current output as “Sometimes”.

observations.text: Within these selected Structural Clarity runs, the senior leader group mean of 74 sits above the manager group mean of 52 and the mean of 49 for people doing the work. Each of those group means rests on 9, 9 and 9 submitted runs respectively, out of 27 submitted runs for this diagnostic, and submitted runs need not come from distinct people.

The saved variation status for these runs is recorded as Two separated score groups, with supplied scores ranging from 49 at the low end to 74 at the high end. This describes how the submitted scores are distributed and does not identify a cause or a position against other organizations.

Asked whether it is clear who owns something they need from another team, all 9 recorded answers from people doing the work were “Often unclear: I ask two or three people first”. To a differently worded senior leader question about telling from the formal structure who is responsible, all 9 recorded answers were “Usually visible with occasional exceptions”. The two questions are not worded alike, so these are separate readings rather than a like-for-like comparison.

hypotheses.text: One operational account reports that when a supplier needs an exception, procurement and the requesting team sometimes each expect the other to decide, and that this participant's experience is mainly routine requests. A senior leader account reports hearing different accounts about who decides exceptions, with their own experience mainly the escalated ones. Together these reported conditions could mean that contested ownership sits in exception handling rather than routine onboarding. A practical check is to pull a set of recent exception cases and record who made the final decision in each.

interpretation.summary: The saved Structural Clarity focus is unclear authority and ownership, and manager answers to those questions record meaningful overlap in responsibilities, decision rights depending on situation and pressure, and frequent time-consuming escalation when accountability is unclear; senior leaders answering differently worded questions record limits of authority mostly clear with occasional testing and unclear accountability occasionally escalated and clearly resolved. observations.text: Across the Structural Clarity runs, the saved focus label is unclear authority and ownership, and the submitted scores fall into two separated groups: the senior leader mean sits well above both the manager and operational means, with the published median between them. These are within-sample scored responses for the submitted runs only, not a measure of how the work actually runs.

Managers answering the Structural Clarity questions recorded that responsibilities overlap meaningfully in ways that create gaps or duplicated work, and that who can decide what depends on the situation and who applies pressure. On resolving unclear accountability, the recorded selection was that it is frequently escalated and takes time. Each of these describes answers to those exact questions from nine recorded answers, not observed events.

Senior leaders answering their own Structural Clarity questions recorded that limits of authority are mostly clear with occasional testing, that accountability usually transfers across boundaries with minor gaps, and that unclear accountability is occasionally escalated and clearly resolved. The wording of these questions differs from the manager set, so the contrast is between question-and-role pairs, not a proven disagreement about the same events.

In Operational Systems, managers recorded that workarounds vary noticeably from person to person, that a new joiner following only the documented process would need substantial coaching on how the work is really done, and that time on administrative maintenance is captured through informal estimates only with no routine records. These are recorded answers to those questions from nine responses each.

Managers answering the Decision Velocity questions recorded that escalations are becoming normal and that the process is noticeably slower than the decision warrants. Senior leaders answering their differently worded questions recorded that work bounces across too many roles or teams and that the process is slightly slower than the decision warrants.

hypotheses.text: One manager account states that team members disagree about whether duplicate entry between the tracker and the vendor system is the main difficulty or whether unclear exceptions create most of the rework, and that the account covers both routine requests and exceptions. An operational account says that for a supplier exception, procurement and the requesting team sometimes each expect the other to decide, while a colleague considers the written responsibility table sufficient. It is possible that difficulty concentrates in exception cases rather than routine files, though one manager account also reports that ownership is clear in practice for some team members. A practical check is to pull a set of recent exception files and recent routine files and compare who actually decided each one.

One operational account says that for an exception the same file is sometimes sent to several approvers with replies awaited in different places, while others on the team say a direct conversation is enough and the writer wants to confirm when the shorter route is authorized. A manager account says exceptions may wait between review meetings and that urgent decisions have also been completed promptly. A senior leader account reports that some managers describe the current route as clear and others describe repeated checks. Waiting might therefore relate to which approval an exception needs rather than to the route as a whole, and the accounts suggest separating urgent from routine cases before assuming a single cause. Reviewing recent exception cases to record which approval each was waiting for would test this.

recommendations.action: Write out each saved focus label beneath its own diagnostic, keeping administrative work with Operational Systems, approval and review requirements with Decision Velocity, unclear authority and ownership with Structural Clarity, and consistency and ability to respond to change with Institutional Performance, so that any follow-up review is scoped to one diagnostic at a time.
